Good morning, Milton. Let me start with the good news. Although the economy is slowing, demand for fine jewelry in the US is still strong.
That's good to hear. And the bad news?
The new tariff on imported jewelry. Because of it, your rings will cost your clients about fifteen percent more.
Even though my clients are loyal, fifteen percent is a lot. And my costs are already higher due to the price of gold.
Yes, gold is the commodity everybody is buying. But there's one thing on your side: the exchange rate. Despite the tariff, a strong dollar means more reais for every sale.
So the dollar pays part of the tariff. Will there be a recession next year?
We don't expect one. Inflation is slowing, and whereas middle-class families lost purchasing power, your buyers didn't.
What do you recommend for the holiday shipment, then?
Ship early. Customs in Miami is slow in November due to the volume, and you don't want your rings to miss the holidays.
Understood. Although the margin will be smaller, I'd rather sell on time than sell late.
Our prices went up because of the price of gold.

Good morning, and welcome to your Monday markets update. Let's start with the dollar. Although many experts expected it to fall this year, the dollar is still strong, and that is good news for exporters who sell in the United States. Next, inflation. Prices in the US rose two point nine percent last year, whereas in Europe the number was closer to two percent. Even though inflation is slowing, many families feel that their purchasing power is smaller than before. Now, gold. Because of the uncertainty in the world, investors are buying more of it, and the price of this commodity reached a new record last week. That is a problem for jewelers, because their raw material is more expensive. Finally, the big question: will there be a recession next year? Most economists say no. Despite the slowdown, demand for luxury goods is still growing, especially among the richest buyers. That's all for today. Have a good week, and see you next Monday.

My name is Ricardo, and I export leather bags from Brazil to the United States and Europe. People think exporting is about the product. It isn't. It's about the world. In 2015, Brazil was in a deep recession. Although my sales in Brazil fell by forty percent, my company survived, because of one decision I had made five years before. I had started selling abroad. Whereas my local clients stopped buying, my American clients kept ordering. And because the real was weak, my products were suddenly cheaper in dollars. The exchange rate saved my business. But the world can also hurt you. Two years ago, a new tariff on leather goods made my prices ten percent higher overnight. Even though my clients liked my bags, some of them changed to cheaper brands. My advice to any exporter is simple. Read the economic news every morning, the same way you read your sales numbers. You cannot control the dollar, a tariff or a recession. But you can be ready for them.
